abstract: Puberty is a sensitive neurodevelopmental period characterized by dramatic increases in adrenal and gonadal hormones, yet how these changes relate to human brain microarchitecture remains unclear. Here, we used restriction spectrum imaging (RSI) to link peripubertal hormone levels to individual differences in brain microarchitecture (i.e., cellular and neurite density) in 7,457 youth (ages 9 to 13 years) from the ABCD Study. Sex- and age-stratified multi-task regression analyses identified microarchitecture patterns jointly associated with physical pubertal maturation and each dehydroepiandrosterone (DHEA), testosterone, estradiol (in female youth), in turn, combining repeated cross-validation with permutation-based feature importance. At ages 9 to 11 years, microarchitecture differences explained 11-13% of pubertal hormone variability in female youth and 4-6% in male youth. Further, microarchitecture features were differentially associated with pubertal hormones. Younger male youth exhibited widespread pubertal hormone-related differences in neurite density that consolidated into fewer, stronger associations with age, while female youth exhibited age-related expansion in pubertal cellular density differences. Anatomically, hormone-relevant microarchitecture consistently included reward processing hubs (e.g., pallidum, accumbens, orbitofrontal cortex). Because animal models suggest that DHEA and testosterone metabolites have opposing effects on GABAergic signaling, we hypothesize that future research should investigate gray matter microarchitecture for insight into pubertal hormone contributions to adolescent refinement of excitatory-inhibitory balance. Ultimately, these findings provide a starting point for investigating how pubertal endocrine changes shape reward circuitry and neurotransmitter systems, with potential implications for the pubertal emergence of sex differences in adolescent psychopathology.
